narrative:
The model determined that you have a 79% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three academic factors, ranked in order of importance. First, your third-year class ranking was the strongest influence. Placing in the bottom decile of your class (compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Second, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile, again far below the typical sixth-decile performance of accepted applicants, added further weight toward a negative outcome. These two performance signals outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the third most important factor. Although this score is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction slightly toward passing. Unfortunately, that modest positive effect could not overcome the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 27, middle-family income, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in the final decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and a competitive test score in a future application would likely change the outcome. Consider academic support programs or a post-baccalaureate course before reapplying.
